rationale:
Every piece today is about GLP-1 medicines, using our proven formats: a named drug (tirzepatide where it's accurate), one plain question, and a practical "you" action. The long-form follows the fact-check rule. Its hook is news (the Cedars-Sinai release on Oct 13), but the body is an evergreen deep-dive built on settled randomized trials (SUMMIT in NEJM 2024, plus STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM), and it hasn't been covered in the last 30 days. S2 is a spin-off of that long-form to send viewers to it.

For timely hooks, two of the three Shorts (S1 and S3) are rising trends. The bootleg "Reta" death reports have the highest momentum on the radar (90), and the S1 angle is new: what's confirmed about the FDA reports, rather than the Sept 30 "not the trial drug" Short. S3 rebuilds the Oct 13 aging carousel as a Short, as planned, now hooked to the drugmaker aging-clock data reported by CNN. Both are "caution" topics, so both get evidence-first angles.

The mix is about 40% rising (S1, S3), 40% evergreen with a timely hook (L1, C1) and 20% evidence-first myth-busting (S2 is the spin-off, and S1 doubles as a myth-bust). That leans slightly away from the 50/30/20 target.

I skipped topics already done in the last 30 days:
- Nails (Oct 1)
- Menopause and orforglipron (Sept 28)
- TRIUMPH-2 as a long-form (Sept 30)
- The pill vs the shot (Oct 13)
- The nausea habits carousel (Sept 30)
- Muscle (Oct 13)

I also skipped vision loss (NAION), because safety scares do worse than our median.

The carousel is a save-worthy checklist that turns our #3 GLP-1 post (surgery/anesthesia, 82 views) into a list format. It gives no stopping or timing advice. Organ spread: the heart appears twice (L1 and S2); otherwise it's online products, aging and surgery. No pillar is used more than twice.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide and semaglutide in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and obesity: an evergreen deep-dive on the randomized trials (SUMMIT for tirzepatide; STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM for semaglutide), with the Cedars-Sinai release (Oct 13) and the new JCEM tirzepatide meta-analysis as the hook
pieces.angle: Evergreen SUMMIT decoder, hooked on SUMMIT itself (not news). Title: 'Did Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Help Heart Failure With Obesity (HFpEF)? What SUMMIT Found'. Segments 1–4 as planned, with every SUMMIT number (absolute event rates per arm, HR with CI, KCCQ change, analysed n, median follow-up) copied from the NEJM 2024 paper. STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM each get their own population and timeframe, labelled 'separate trials, not head to head'. Segment 5: 'What's next': (a) a confirmed 2026 meta-analysis with its real journal (e.g. Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice 2026, PubMed 42442557), described as pooled trial data; and (b) optionally the Cedars-Sinai European Heart Journal study (Oct 13, 2026), described ONLY as 'an early animal study in rats and minipigs, not a human result'. Do not mention its low doses and do not imply any human dosing. Segment 6: GI side effects with placebo rates. Segment 7: 'As of Oct 2026, tirzepatide is not FDA-approved to treat heart failure. Lilly withdrew its heart-failure application in 2025 after FDA asked for more data. It is approved for chronic weight management and obstructive sleep apnea.' Segment 8: cardiologist/prescriber questions, label contraindications. No dosing, switching or stopping advice. Close with 'talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you'.
pieces.working_title: Does Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Help Heart Failure? What the SUMMIT Trial Found
pieces.why:
Named-drug trial decoders are our proven long-form winner. The topic rests on well-documented NEJM randomized trials, so it can pass the fact-check in depth, and it has a fresh Oct 13 hook. | fact-check: The core topic is sound and evergreen. SUMMIT (NEJM 2024, NCT04847557) is real and fits a long-form trial decoder. Three problems with the hook need fixing first.
(1) The CEDARS-SINAI OCT 13 WORK IS AN ANIMAL STUDY, NOT OBSERVATIONAL. The Newswise release dated Oct 13, 2026 (European Heart Journal) tested LOW-DOSE semaglutide in rats and minipigs with an HFpEF-like condition. It reports less heart stiffness, enlargement and scarring without much weight loss. Calling it 'observational work … linked to' is wrong. Its 'low doses' framing could also read as a microdosing nudge, which is a banned topic. It may appear only as preclinical animal research, with no low-dose emphasis and no human implication.
(2) THE 'NEW JCEM TIRZEPATIDE META-ANALYSIS' COULD NOT BE VERIFIED. The October 2026 JCEM issue shows no such paper. The 2026 tirzepatide meta-analyses I found are in Diabetes Research and Clinical Practice (PubMed 42442557, Sept 2026: MACE OR 0.87; all-cause mortality OR 0.84) and Endocrine Practice ('Tirzepatide Beyond Diabetes and Obesity', 17 RCTs, which reports HFpEF HR 0.62, i.e. SUMMIT). Neither is JCEM. Either name a confirmed paper with its real journal or drop it.
(3) STATUS: tirzepatide has NO heart-failure indication. Lilly withdrew its HFpEF application in May 2025 after FDA asked for another trial. The label (revised Aug 2026, per secondary sources) covers chronic weight management and obstructive sleep apnea. Say this plainly. Prescribing for HFpEF is off-label.
The title should name HFpEF + obesity, not 'heart failure' in general. SUMMIT says nothing about reduced-EF heart failure. Keep STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM separate and not head to head. Keep the population for each segment exact: SUMMIT included people with and without T2D.

pieces.topic: Bootleg 'Reta': CBS News (Oct 13) reported that the FDA received two death reports after people took products sold as retatrutide
pieces.angle: Answer within 10 s: 'Retatrutide isn't approved anywhere as of Oct 2026. CBS reported two deaths reported to the FDA after people took products claiming to be it. It hasn't been established that the products caused the deaths, and nobody knows what the vials contained.' Credit the details to CBS News and keep its exact wording. Explain that the trial results came from Lilly's drug, made and tested under medical supervision, while products sold online may not match their labels. Cite the FDA's own warning page on unapproved GLP-1 products directly. Never name a seller, show a vial, or mention doses or sourcing. Better route: ask your prescriber about approved options or a clinical trial. Close with the prescriber line. 170 words or fewer.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: the SUMMIT result in one number
pieces.angle: Title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound) in Heart Failure With Obesity: What SUMMIT Found #shorts'. Within 10 s: the SUMMIT composite of cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure, as absolute % per arm (tirzepatide vs placebo) plus the HR, copied from NEJM 2024. On-screen pill: 'adults with HFpEF + obesity (BMI 30+) · vs placebo · ~2 years · NEJM 2024'. One line: HFpEF = a stiff heart that doesn't fill well. One line: common GI side effects (nausea, diarrhoea, constipation), usually mild to moderate. Status line: 'As of Oct 2026, tirzepatide isn't FDA-approved to treat heart failure. It's approved for weight management and sleep apnea.' Point to the L1 deep-dive. Close with 'talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you'. 170 words or fewer.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) and Heart Failure: What SUMMIT Found #shorts
pieces.why:
Spin-off of L1, to drive traffic to the long video. It uses the proven format of a named drug plus one number, with tirzepatide in the title. | fact-check: The SUMMIT one-number Short is a good fit and pairs with L1. Two changes are needed.
(1) The status line must say clearly that tirzepatide is NOT FDA-approved for heart failure as of Oct 2026. Lilly withdrew its HFpEF application in 2025. Saying only 'date any approval status' risks implying an indication.
(2) The working title says 'Heart Failure' in general. SUMMIT studied only HFpEF + obesity (BMI 30+), so the title must name that population.
Secondary sources give the composite figure as a 38% relative reduction (HR 0.62). The script must pair it with the absolute event rates per arm from the NEJM paper, as the craft rules require. Note that SUMMIT included adults with and without T2D.

pieces.topic: Do GLP-1 medicines slow biological aging? Aging-clock data reported by drugmakers (CNN Oct 13, MIT Technology Review Oct 6)
pieces.angle: Title: 'Do Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) or Semaglutide (Ozempic) Slow Aging? What's Actually Shown #shorts'. Within 10 s: 'Not shown yet. These are early aging-clock readings the drugmakers presented, in people with overweight, obesity or diabetes. They're not a lifespan result.' Aging clock = blood or protein markers that estimate 'biological age', not years lived. Experts say these clocks are still in development. Figure: 'Novo Nordisk told MIT Technology Review the difference vs placebo was around 2 to 3 years, depending on the clock and organ.' Caveat: 'Lilly told CNN the effects are mostly due to blood-sugar and weight changes.' Expert line: 'An aging researcher told CNN it's too early to take these drugs just to live longer.' What IS shown: SELECT (fewer heart attacks, strokes and CV deaths in adults with heart disease and overweight/obesity, without diabetes) and FLOW (kidney outcomes in adults with T2D and chronic kidney disease). One line on common GI side effects. No #antiaging, #longevity or brand hashtags. Close with 'talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you'.
pieces.working_title: Does Mounjaro or Ozempic Slow Aging? What the Data Actually Shows #shorts
pieces.why:
A rising topic (momentum 80) as a 'what does it do to my body?' question with named drugs. It rebuilds the Oct 13 carousel as a Short, as the playbook asks. | fact-check: The topic is legitimate and the planned framing is cautious. However, the figure and its attribution are wrong.
- MIT Technology Review (Oct 6, 2026) quotes Novo's Nikolaj Roed: overall difference 'around two to three years'.
- CNN (Oct 13) reports Novo researchers saying semaglutide lowered the heart's biological age by 2–4 years vs placebo, and other organs by 1–4 years.
So the '2–3 years, as CNN reported' credit is wrong.
The weight-loss caveat is split:
- Lilly's Kevin Duffin told CNN the effects are 'mostly due to' blood-sugar reduction and weight loss.
- Novo said its effects were 'not completely explained by weight loss'.
Use both. Do not claim one caveat applies to all the data.
CNN's caution comes from Dr. James Kirkland: 'people could overread some of this stuff'. He says it's too early to use these drugs solely to live longer, and that clocks 'are still in development' and 'vary tremendously from day to day'.
These are exploratory, company-presented biomarker data (ARDD 2026 meeting), not peer-reviewed lifespan outcomes. Keep that hedge.
Risk: the topic can encourage off-label 'anti-aging' use in people without obesity or diabetes. Say explicitly that it was studied in people with overweight/obesity or diabetes.
The title with two brands leans toward an ad. Lead with generics.
Populations for the proven benefits: SELECT and FLOW as listed in the angle are correct.

pieces.topic: Having surgery, an endoscopy or a procedure while on semaglutide or tirzepatide: a checklist of what to tell your care team (hook: Oct 12 systematic review on blood-sugar control around cardiac surgery in adults with T2D)
pieces.angle:
Hook on GLIMPSE, not the unverified cardiac-surgery review. Title: 'Surgery or Endoscopy on Semaglutide or Tirzepatide? 4 Things to Tell Your Care Team'.
Slide 1: the question.
Slide 2: 'These medicines can slow stomach emptying (label wording). In a 2025 UK study of 47,000+ adults having anaesthesia, regurgitation or aspiration was recorded in 1.41% of people who'd used a GLP-1-based medicine in the past 3 months vs 0.12% of non-users (19 of 1,348 vs 57 of 45,691). Most events were regurgitation. The study shows a link, not proof of cause.' Source tag: GLIMPSE.
Slide 3: tell your anesthesia team and prescriber which medicine you take and when you last took it.
Slide 4: mention any nausea, vomiting or fullness in the days before.
Slide 5: 'If you have diabetes, ask how your blood sugar will be managed around the procedure.' Use no source tag unless it cites a confirmed guideline.
Slide 6: 'Guidance differs between professional groups. Follow your team's plan, and don't stop or change your medicine on your own.'
Slide 7: 'talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you'.
A source tag on every claim slide, using direct canonical URLs.
pieces.working_title: Surgery on Semaglutide or Tirzepatide? 5 Things to Tell Your Care Team
pieces.why:
It turns our #3 GLP-1 post (anesthesia, 82 views) into a checklist format people save. The hook is the systematic review published Oct 12. | fact-check: GLIMPSE is verified (UK, 119 hospitals, Sept–Dec 2025, led by Kariem El-Boghdadly). Regurgitation or aspiration occurred in 19 of 1,348 people who had used a GLP-1-based medicine in the previous 3 months (1.41%) vs 57 of 45,691 non-users (0.12%). Of the 19 events, 17 were regurgitation and 2 were pulmonary aspiration. It is an observational association.
I could NOT verify the 'Oct 12 systematic review on blood-sugar control around cardiac surgery in adults with T2D'. What I found on GLP-1s in cardiac surgery concerns giving liraglutide around surgery as a glucose-control tool, which is a different question from patients already on semaglutide or tirzepatide. Drop it as the hook unless the exact paper is confirmed, and don't let slide 5 imply that GLP-1s should be used or continued around surgery.
The title says '5 Things', but the checklist has 4 action slides (3–6). Make the count match.
No stopping, pausing or timing advice is correct. 'Say when you last took it' is fine because it's information-giving.
Note: the playbook says carousels are dead (Instagram reach 0–3, n=15) and recommends rebuilding this exact topic as a Short. That's the owner's call, but the content is approvable either way.
